summary: A Best Current Practice describing how to stop default-configured recursive name servers from being used as reflectors in denial of service attacks. It recommends configuration measures to reduce the attack. An attacker can make such servers send large replies to a victim, so limiting who may ask them helps.

eli5.summary: If a shop answers any stranger's question, a bully could trick it into shouting answers at someone else. This says to answer only your own customers.

questions: what is a dns reflector attack
what is an open recursive resolver
subtitle: How to stop open DNS resolvers from being turned into amplifiers for denial of service attacks.

tldr.problem: Recursive nameservers that answer anyone on the Internet can be tricked, using forged source addresses, into sending large DNS replies to a victim.
tldr.mechanism: Operators should serve recursion only to the intended clients, using address ACLs, incoming interface, signed queries (TSIG or SIG(0)), a local cache or a VPN, and turn recursion off on authoritative-only servers.
tldr.outcome: Recursive service is no longer meant to be open by default, but the RFC says the only real fix is wide-scale ingress filtering (BCP 38) against spoofed addresses.

facts.label: Default rule
facts.value: SHOULD NOT offer recursion to external networks

today: RFC 5358 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 140) and, according to the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its core advice, to serve recursion only to intended clients, stands as written.

sections.title: Why Open Resolvers Are a Problem
sections.content:
RFC 5358 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 140) about reflector attacks, a kind of denial of service (DoS) attack. The RFC says DNS has been named as a major factor in generating massive amounts of attack traffic. This is not due to a flaw in the design of DNS or its implementations, except that DNS relies heavily on UDP, which is easy to abuse.

The attacks mostly use open recursive nameservers, which are reachable because of common default configurations. Because a small query can yield a large response, the reflected traffic towards the victim is greatly amplified.

Authoritative servers that do not provide recursion can also be used as amplifiers, but the potential is greatly reduced, and they cannot practically be restricted to a subset of the Internet. So the recommendations cover recursive nameservers only.
sections.eli5: Some DNS servers answer anybody who asks, and a short question can get a very long answer. Bad people use that to flood someone with answers they never asked for.

sections.title: How the Reflector Attack Works
sections.content:
Most DNS traffic is stateless by design, so an attacker can proceed in four steps:

  1. Configure a record in any zone they have access to, normally with large RDATA and a large Time to Live (TTL).
  2. Using clients on networks that do not follow BCP 38, craft a query that carries the victim's address as its source and send it to an open recursive nameserver.
  3. Each open recursive nameserver resolves the name, caches the record and sends it to the victim. After the first lookup the authoritative servers are normally no longer needed, and the record stays cached for the TTL even if it is deleted from the zone.
  4. Depending on the implementation, cleaning up the zone may be a way to clear the cached record, possibly by luring the nameserver into looking up the same name again.

With an open recursive nameserver that supports EDNS0 (RFC 2671), the amplification factor (response packet size divided by query packet size) could be around 80. The RFC notes that a relatively small army of clients and open servers could generate gigabits of traffic.

Since each participant sends only a low volume of packets, it is unlikely any one of them would notice their involvement from traffic changes. The RFC also expects authoritative servers to become more useful for this as DNSSEC and NAPTR records (used in ENUM services) make responses longer.
sections.eli5: The prankster writes a very long note, then phones many helpful librarians pretending to be the victim. Each librarian sends the long note to the victim, so the victim gets buried in mail.

sections.title: Why Servers Ended Up Open
sections.content:
The RFC says the attack is only possible because BCP 38 is not deployed everywhere, but it is easier to carry out for historical reasons. When the Internet was a closer-knit community, some nameserver implementations shipped with default configurations that, used as recursive nameservers, made the server accessible to all hosts on the Internet.

That was convenient for years, but the RFC argues it is now much better to focus a nameserver on its intended audience, such as a university campus, an enterprise or an ISP's customers. Operators of small networks and private servers are a particular target of the advice because they are more likely to keep the defaults shipped by implementors.
sections.eli5: Long ago everyone knew each other, so shops left their doors open. Today the doors should be open only for your own customers.

sections.title: Ways to Limit Who Can Ask
sections.content:
The general recommendation is to provide recursive lookup service only to the intended clients. The RFC lists several ways to authorize clients:

  • IP address based authorization: filter the source address of queries through an Access Control List (ACL). This is easy when the service area is a fairly fixed address range protected against external address spoofing, usually the local network.
  • Incoming interface: choose clients by the interface the query arrived on. This is especially useful for SOHO devices such as broadband routers with embedded recursive nameservers.
  • Signed queries: TSIG (RFC 2845) or SIG(0) (RFC 2931). This is less error prone and suits roaming clients, but very few stub resolvers can sign queries, so it usually means running a local caching nameserver or forwarder that signs them.
  • Mobile users: run a local caching nameserver on the device or use a Virtual Private Network to a trusted server.
sections.eli5: You can check a guest list, check which door someone came through, ask for a secret password, or give travelers their own helper. Each way keeps strangers out.

sections.title: Turning Recursion Off and Filtering Spoofing
sections.content:
Nameservers that do not need to give recursive service, such as authoritative-only servers, should have recursion turned off completely. In general it is a good idea to keep recursive and authoritative services separate as much as practical, depending on local circumstances.

Even so, operators should consider ingress filtering (BCP 38, RFC 2827) in routers so that address spoofing is not a viable course of action. For more complex setups, "Ingress Filtering for Multihomed Networks" (BCP 84, RFC 3704) may be a useful additional reference.

The one normative rule: by default, nameservers SHOULD NOT offer recursive service to external networks.
sections.eli5: Servers that do not need to answer questions for others should simply stop doing it. And the post office should refuse letters with fake return addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it creates no new security issues for the DNS protocol; it deals with a weakness in implementations.

For SIG(0), the RFC warns about its computational expense, since it uses public key cryptography rather than the symmetric keys of TSIG. Finding the right keys needs mechanisms similar to those for deploying TSIG, or DNSSEC signatures (RRSIGs) over KEY records if published in DNS, which in turn requires managing DNSSEC trust anchors.
sections.eli5: Secret passwords take work to hand out and check, so plan for that before using them.
